errors.english: ### Chapter Twenty-one: Examination of Coming into Being and Dissolution
errors.why: This is the closing colophon of chapter 21; rendered as a heading it makes the following Tathāgata verses (chapter 22) appear to belong to chapter 21.

fix.find: ### Chapter Twenty-one: Examination of Coming into Being and Dissolution
fix.replace: This was the twenty-first chapter, the Examination of Coming into Being and Dissolution.

errors.english: then he would be a basis for them now; but since he depends on them, he is contingent upon that dependence.
errors.why: MMK 22.5: such a Tathāgata would only now come to depend on the aggregates, and having depended would thereby come to be; he is not a basis for them.

fix.find: then he would be a basis for them now; but since he depends on them, he is contingent upon that dependence.
fix.replace: then he would only now come to depend on them, and having depended, he would thereby come to be.

note: Verses of MMK 21-22 are mostly rendered correctly, but the chapter colophon is turned into an opening heading and 22.5 is misconstrued.
Faithful rendering of Avalokitavrata's argument against suffering made by another, including the conventional/ultimate distinction.

errors.english: This is because one intends to establish the (sadhya) the thesis or what is to be proven solely through the very similarity with the example itself.
errors.why: The point is that the similarity itself is held to be the means of proof (sādhana), so there is no source distinct from it; the inserted sādhya gloss obscures this.

errors.english: The claim that "whatever exists is a qualifier of the subject" is therefore unreasonable.
errors.why: Likely: what is actually stated (in the compound) is a qualifier of the dharmin, so this reading is not right; not a general claim about whatever exists.

note: A careful rendering of a grammatical argument about the ablative in the hetu definition, with minor blurring in two places.

errors.english: This clarifies that the point claiming "the eye is the very essence of seeing" is flawed due to an uncertain reason.
errors.why: The commentary says the opponent's charge of an inconclusive reason, made to establish that the eye has the nature of seeing, cannot succeed through the fire example; it does not say the eye thesis has an inconclusive reason.
This continues the opponent's objection (what the Madhyamaka's argument amounts to); it is not a reply, and the heading mark is spurious.

note: Generally sound, including the gone/not-gone analysis applied to burning, but the opening objection-reply structure is blurred.

errors.english: Since there is no birth, there is no permanence. In this context, if something were to be born, it would be permanent; but since that is not the case, there is no permanence. Because there is no cessation
errors.why: The Tibetan states the no-birth/no-permanence argument only once, after the no-cessation/no-annihilation one; the English duplicates it.

fix.find: Since there is no birth, there is no permanence. In this context, if something were to be born, it would be permanent; but since that is not the case, there is no permanence. Because there is no cessation

errors.english: There is "no birth" because it is untenable for there to be a transition
errors.why: Probably: arising is untenable without transition (’pho ba med par), not that transition is untenable.

note: The sūtra dialogue and the ordering argument are rendered well apart from a duplicated sentence.

errors.english: Is one attempting to establish the independence of speech itself, or is one attempting to establish a (prasanga) consequentialist argument?
errors.why: smra ba nyid is vaktṛtva, 'being a speaker' (the reason under discussion), and rang dbang du sgrub pa means proving it as an independent (svatantra) inference, not proving the independence of speech; the same error recurs as 'act of speech'.

fix.find: Is one attempting to establish the independence of speech itself, or is one attempting to establish a (prasanga) consequentialist argument?
fix.replace: Does one intend to put forward [the reason] 'being a speaker' (vaktṛtva) as an independent (svatantra) proof, or as a (prasanga) consequence?

errors.english: In establishing that consequence, if one does not analyze, one might find simple pleasure in mere scripture.
errors.why: 'Pleasing only when unexamined' qualifies the scripture by which the property is well known to the other party; it is not a separate statement about finding pleasure.
No heading appears on this side; the text begins mid-sentence.

note: The argument's key reason, 'being a speaker', is systematically rendered as 'speech/act of speaking', and one clause is misparsed.

errors.english: A cow is not the substantial cause of another cow
errors.why: ba men is a buffalo/gayal: a buffalo is not the substantial cause of a cow, because they are different kinds.

fix.find: A cow is not the substantial cause of another cow
fix.replace: A buffalo is not the substantial cause of a cow

errors.english: To show that there is no difference in the way they appear as separate entities
errors.why: The point is that the separate appearance and other marks that prove distinctness apply equally (no difference between the cases) to mind and body.

errors.english: shows they support one another's existence
errors.why: The fire is shown to sustain the molten state of the copper; this is not mutual support.

note: The thread on substantial vs circumstantial causes is followable, but the opening example is mistranslated and a few clauses are misconstrued.

errors.english: On the basis of the intense clinging of the mind
errors.why: In apoha theory lhag par zhen pa / zhen pa is adhyavasāya, conceptual determination, not affective clinging (also 'in relation to clinging' below).

fix.find: On the basis of the intense clinging of the mind
fix.replace: On the basis of the determination (adhyavasāya) of the cognition

note: A sound rendering of the apoha argument about non-relation as generality, apart from the key term adhyavasāya.

errors.why: brtse ba is compassion/kindness, not equanimity.

note: Faithful account of mantras as conventions made by a powerful person, with the poet analogy; one term is wrong.

errors.english: if the community is empowered through the ritual motion
errors.why: What is 'blessed'/formally set aside (adhiṣṭhita) through the jñapti is the offences, as the following lines show, not the community; 'empowered' is also a poor rendering of this Vinaya procedure.

note: A difficult Vinaya passage on offences and the validity of the saṅgha is rendered sensibly, with correct offence classes.
